q: What is a tax deduction?
r: An amount that lowers the income on which tax is calculated
The standard deduction is an example.
w: An amount that is subtracted from the tax after it is figured
An extra penalty added for filing late
A refund sent by a bank on request
That is not a tax term.

q: What is a tax credit?
r: An amount that reduces the tax owed dollar for dollar
Credits are powerful.
w: An amount that lowers taxable income

q: Which is worth more: a $500 tax deduction or a $500 tax credit, if your tax rate is 12%?
r: The $500 credit
It cuts tax by $500, while the deduction saves $60.

q: What is the standard deduction?
r: A fixed amount that most taxpayers can subtract from income
It simplifies filing.
w: A deduction available only to businesses
A fee for filing a return
A deduction that must be itemized
It is the alternative to itemizing.

q: When is the usual federal income tax filing deadline?
r: April 15, or the next business day
Extensions can give more time to file, not to pay.

q: A student earned $3,000 from a summer job and had $0 tax withheld. What should they do?
r: Check whether they must file a return and claim any refund
Low earners may owe little or nothing.
w: Pay a random amount to be safe
Let their employer file for them

q: What is gross pay versus net pay?
r: Gross pay is before deductions; net pay is after deductions
Net pay is take-home pay.
w: Gross pay is after deductions; net pay is before

q: Gross pay is $1,200 and deductions total $240. What percent of gross pay is deducted?
r: $240 divided by $1,200 equals 0.20.

q: What is a raise?
r: An increase in pay
Employers may give raises for performance.

q: A worker earning $15 an hour gets a 4% raise. What is the new hourly wage?
What is the difference between renting and buying a home?
r: Renting means paying to use a place; buying means owning it
Owners also pay upkeep and taxes.
w: Renting means owning; buying means borrowing from a friend

q: Which cost does a renter usually NOT pay compared with an owner?
r: Major repairs to the building
The landlord handles them.

q: What is a security deposit?
r: Money a landlord holds against damage or unpaid rent
It may be returned when you leave.
w: A monthly fee for living in a place

q: A tenant pays a $600 deposit and leaves the apartment in good condition. What should happen?
r: The deposit is returned, minus any valid charges
Deposits cover damage or unpaid rent.
w: The landlord keeps it no matter what
It becomes rent for next month
That is not how it works.

q: What is a lease?
r: A legal agreement to rent property for a set time
It states rent and rules.
w: A loan to buy a house

q: Why should you read a lease before signing?
r: To understand rent, fees, rules and how to end it
Surprises can be costly.
w: To make the document last longer
To avoid talking to the landlord
To make the landlord more friendly

q: What is a used-car history report for?
r: Checking past accidents, owners and title problems
It helps avoid bad purchases.
w: Setting the price of new cars

q: Which step best protects you when buying a used car?
r: Get an independent mechanic to inspect it
An expert can find hidden problems.
w: Buy the first car you see

q: What is the total cost of owning a car?
r: Purchase price plus insurance, fuel, repairs and other costs
Ownership costs go beyond the price.

q: A car costs $200 a month in payments and $150 a month in insurance, fuel and upkeep. What is the monthly cost?
r: $200 plus $150 equals $350.

q: What is a want that can be reduced to save money?
r: Dining out every day
It is a variable want.

q: Dining out costs $12 a day for 20 days a month. If cut to 5 days, how much is saved monthly?
r: 15 days times $12 equals $180.

q: What is a sinking fund?
r: Money set aside regularly for a planned future expense
It spreads out a large cost.
w: A fund that earns no interest

q: You want $1,200 for a trip in 12 months. How much should you set aside monthly?
r: $1,200 divided by 12 equals $100.

q: What is the benefit of keeping savings in an account separate from spending money?
r: It reduces the temptation to spend savings
Out of sight, out of mind.
w: It removes the need to budget
It makes the money tax free

q: What is an emergency fund goal for most households?
r: Three to six months of essential expenses
It cushions job loss or repairs.

q: Essential expenses are $1,800 a month. What is a three-month emergency fund?
r: $1,800 times 3 equals $5,400.

q: What is interest rate risk for savers?
r: The risk that rates fall and new deposits earn less
It affects savings yields.
w: The risk that a bank fails
The risk that you forget the PIN

q: Which choice best protects savings from both loss and inflation over many years?
r: A mix of safe savings and diversified long-term investments
It balances safety and growth.
w: All money in one risky stock

q: What is a credit report error you should dispute?
r: An account you never opened listed in your name
It could signal identity theft.
w: An account you opened and repaid
A late payment you really made

q: After disputing a credit report error, what must the credit bureau generally do?
r: Investigate and correct or remove inaccurate items
The law requires an investigation.
w: Charge you a fee to look

q: What is a credit limit increase?
r: A higher borrowing limit on a card
It can lower utilization if spending stays the same.

q: Your balance is $600 on a $2,000 limit. The limit rises to $3,000. What happens to utilization if the balance stays the same?
r: It falls from 30% to 20%
$600 divided by $3,000 equals 20 percent.

q: What is a minimum payment trap?
r: Paying only the minimum so the debt lasts long and costs more interest
Balances shrink slowly.
w: Paying more than the minimum each month

q: Which choice reduces interest costs on a card balance the fastest?
r: Paying more than the minimum each month
Principal falls faster.

q: What is a personal loan?
r: Money borrowed for a personal purpose that is repaid in installments
It is often unsecured.

q: A $3,000 loan at 8% simple interest for 1 year costs how much interest?
What is a home equity loan?
r: A loan secured by the value you own in your home
The home is collateral.
w: A loan for a car only
A grant that is not repaid

q: What is a deductible's role in lowering premiums?
r: Taking on more of the first costs yourself lowers the insurer's risk
So premiums can be lower.
w: It removes the insurer from your claims
The insurer still pays above it.
It has no effect on premiums

q: Which situation shows a good reason to choose a higher deductible?
r: You have an emergency fund to cover the first costs
You can afford the extra risk.
w: You have no savings at all
You could not cover the deductible.
You want the highest possible premium

q: What is insurance fraud?
r: Lying or exaggerating to get an insurer to pay
It is illegal.

q: A person reports a car stolen when it was sold. What is this?
r: Insurance fraud
It is a false claim.

q: What is a replacement cost policy?
r: A policy that pays to replace items at current prices
Actual cash value pays less.
w: A policy that pays only the item's depreciated value

q: A 5-year-old laptop worth $200 is stolen. A new one costs $900. Which policy type pays more?
r: Replacement cost
It pays close to the cost of a new one.

q: What is a home inventory for insurance?
r: A list or photos of belongings with their values
It helps with claims.
w: A list of home repair tools

q: After a fire, why is a home inventory helpful?
r: It speeds up and supports your insurance claim
It proves what you owned.

q: What is a retirement account's tax advantage?
r: Taxes may be deferred or reduced on contributions or earnings
Rules depend on the account type.
w: No taxes ever apply to any account
The account pays for your groceries

q: Why is it important to take full advantage of an employer 401(k) match?
r: It adds free money to your retirement savings
Skipping it leaves money unclaimed.
w: It lowers your income tax to zero
It lets you withdraw anytime without penalty

q: What is portfolio diversification across asset classes?
r: Holding different types such as stocks, bonds and cash
It spreads risk.
w: Holding only one type of asset

q: An investor holds only stock in the company that employs them. What extra risk do they take?
r: Both their job and savings depend on one company
Failure would hit both.
w: Less risk than a diversified fund
